description: We are Donbas Solutions, a four-person software engineering team from the Faculty of Informatics and Computer Engineering (FICE) at Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (NTUU KPI). Our core strength lies in full-stack development, data engineering, and building scalable, user-friendly web applications from the ground up.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a free, public web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared sky survey into short animations anyone can explore. Users enter a star name or sky coordinates, and the tool gathers every SPHEREx visit of that patch of sky. Each visit is stacked per detector, aligned on one shared grid and shown with one brightness scale, so moving and changing objects stand out at a glance.

Blinking, a difference mode and expected-position markers make motion visible. Spectra and light curves, measured from the same images, show how a star’s brightness changes with wavelength and time. Overlays add Gaia DR3 stars, data-quality flags and context from other surveys. Every view can be shared or embedded with a single link.

We tested the tool on all five challenge targets. The motion of nearby stars it measures closely matches catalogue predictions, it detects the brightening of a variable star, and our photometry agrees with IRSA’s own tool.

SPHEREx collects far more data than anyone can inspect by hand. SPHEREx Blink lets anyone explore it in a browser, without code or astronomy software, and never presents saturated or incomplete data as a clean measurement.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Blink is a free public web tool that shows how any patch of sky changes across NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey. Enter a star name or RA/Dec coordinates, choose a field of view (2–30′), and the tool builds a time sequence from every SPHEREx visit of that spot. Users can:

  • play it as a blink animation or flip between any two visits;
  • switch to difference mode (later minus earlier), where a moving star leaves a blue spot where it was and an orange one where it is now;
  • see where a known star is expected on each date, with Gaia DR3 stars overlaid at each frame’s epoch;
  • show data-quality flags (saturated, bad and artifact pixels);
  • view the target’s spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm and its light curve, measured from the same exposures;
  • compare with 2MASS, AllWISE and DSS2 in an Aladin Lite sky panel;
  • share or embed any view, since the whole state lives in the URL.

How it works


The backend finds every SPHEREx exposure of the position in NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive. It picks up new data releases automatically. Instead of whole 62 MB files, it downloads only the pixels around the target from the public AWS copy, about 4 MB per image. It then removes the zodiacal (interplanetary dust) glow and the local background, masks flagged pixels, reprojects every image onto one north-up grid, and stacks each visit per detector. All frames share one brightness scale, so a real change shows up as a change and nothing is faked by contrast. The browser receives raw pixel arrays and draws, stretches and subtracts them itself.

Results

We tested the tool on all five challenge targets. Barnard’s Star moves 1.65 px (10.3″) in about a year, against 1.67 px predicted from its catalogue proper motion. ε Indi B moves 1.07 px (6.7″) over 1.4 years, against 1.05 px predicted. RW Aurigae brightens 2.5× at 0.75 µm (16.6σ). R Draconis is saturated in every exposure, and the tool says so instead of showing false numbers. Our photometry of an unsaturated test star agrees with IRSA’s own Spectrophotometry Tool to a median ratio of 0.998.

Benefits and impact

Anyone with a browser can see in seconds how the sky changed, with no Python, no FITS files and no login. The tool is meant to help the public, students and educators inspect real SPHEREx observations, decide what deserves a closer look, and share a finding with one link.

Creativity

SPHEREx sees a different wavelength across each detector, which normally makes comparing images hard. We turned that into a feature: the same exposures that build the blink also give the target’s spectrum and a light curve compared at matched wavelengths. The five test targets ship as bundles of real data, so they work even when the archive is down.

Factors we considered

  • SPHEREx pixels are 6.2″, so even the fastest stars move only 1–2 px a year. We use the longest time baseline and difference mode to make this motion visible.
  • Wavelength varies across each image, so frames are compared per detector, and incomplete coverage is flagged.
  • Saturated or masked data is never shown as a clean measurement.
  • The archive was often overloaded during the hackathon, so we added retries, caching, several data sources and an offline fallback.
  • Proper-motion markers show predicted positions. Searches beyond the five test targets depend on archive coverage. SPHEREx Blink is a visual investigation tool, not an automated all-sky search, and it makes no claim to have found Planet X.

Tools

  • Python 3.13, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, photutils.
  • React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Aladin Lite.
  • Docker, GitHub Actions, Azure Container Apps.
  • Code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code (Anthropic). The running tool uses no AI.
